DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.628.setting: Community mental health resource centre (local CMHT)
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.628.standard: NICE guidance: lipid profile at baseline, 3 months and annually, and cardiovascular risk assessment with a validated tool (QRISK3 or ASSIGN score)

cycle1.result: Lipid profile done in the past 12 months in 22/27 (81.1%); cardiovascular risk assessed in 1/27 (3.70%); lipid results communicated to GP in 4/22 (18.18%).

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.628.intervention: Proposed structured process: clozapine clinic nurse creates an electronic task for the medic to review results, calculate cardiovascular risk and communicate lipids and risk to the GP in the annual review letter. Re-audit planned after 12 months.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2024.628.other_findings: Of 40 patients on clozapine, 13 were excluded (on statins, recently started, or outside age 30–74). Of those tested, 13/22 (59.9%) had total cholesterol above 5 mmol/L.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.57.topic: Carboplatin therapeutic drug monitoring in children
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.57.standard: Local carboplatin protocol requirements for age criteria, baseline audiology, creatinine clearance and pharmacokinetic monitoring before administration

cycle1.dates: Data collected December 2018 to January 2019 for patients treated from 2017 to present
cycle1.result: Audiology done in 85.7% (n=6) but at baseline pre-treatment in only 28.6% (n=2); creatinine checked before first course in 71.4%; 20/26 courses (76.9%) had PK monitoring with dose modification as per protocol; 2 (29%) patients did not meet the age criteria for PK monitoring.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.57.intervention: Recommended information for all practitioners on monitoring requirements and production of an SOP.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.57.other_findings: Seven patients received 26 courses of carboplatin; patients were often monitored beyond 3 months of age throughout treatment.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.114.topic: Live vaccination in children on immunosuppression
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.114.setting: Royal Manchester Children's Hospital paediatric rheumatology service, tertiary centre
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.114.standard: 2017 Public Health England / Green Book guidance supporting MMR and varicella vaccination on methotrexate and case-by-case after MDT assessment

cycle1.result: 81 vaccinations (38 VZV, 43 MMR) recommended by the vaccine MDT; 34/81 (42%) administered (20/38 VZV and 14/43 MMR).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.114.intervention: Recommended strengthening follow-up pathways, standardising communication and reinforcing primary care engagement.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.114.other_findings: Four VZV-negative patients developed varicella; 2 needed hospital admission and one developed acute kidney injury. Seven patients received prophylactic aciclovir.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/kez416.025.setting: Alder Hey Children's Hospital paediatric rheumatology department, tertiary centre
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/kez416.025.standard: Blood monitoring guidelines for methotrexate, etanercept and adalimumab: starters must meet 6 criteria (frequency, FBC, LFTs, renal function, varicella and measles immunity); maintenance patients 4 criteria

cycle1.result: Over 60% of patients on methotrexate not monitored according to guidelines.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/kez416.025.intervention: A blood clerk was introduced to the team to chase patients for blood results.

cycle2.result: 76/216 (35%) appropriately monitored, similar to the previous audit. Main failure was delayed blood timing (50% methotrexate, 65% maintenance biologics); missing varicella/measles immunity documentation in 42% of biologic starters.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/kez416.025.other_findings: 72% of patients with inappropriate test frequency received a blood clerk intervention; allowing for appointment time after intervention, appropriate monitoring rose to 64% (methotrexate) and 67% (maintenance biologics). No correlation with distance to centre in the re-audit.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.11.topic: Acute pain assessment and analgesia timing in children
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.11.setting: Paediatric wards excluding intensive care and day surgery
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.11.standard: Locally developed MDT standards: 80% of severe pain scores to get analgesia within 20 minutes and mild/moderate within 30 minutes with timely reassessment; 80% on regular analgesia to have pain scored at least 4-hourly; 90% on strong opioids co-prescribed naloxone

cycle1.result: Analgesia given in the same hour for 58% (34/59) severe and 30% (28/92) mild/moderate pain scores; pain reassessed within 60 minutes after 52% (37/71) and 34% (31/92) of administrations; 15/18 (83%) on regular analgesia assessed at least 4-hourly; of 11 on strong opioids 45% had no naloxone, 27% fully prescribed and 27% for respiratory depression only.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.11.intervention: Planned: specific timing guidance added to the revised guideline, with medical and nursing training sessions.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.11.other_findings: Observation charts allowed 15-minute pain score documentation but only hourly recordings were seen.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znac404.077.standard: NICE quality standards / CG141 for acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding

cycle1.result: Blatchford score used in 12.5% (5/40); endoscopy <24 hours in stable patients 91.4% (32/35); PPI for non-variceal bleeds 74.4% (29/39); aspirin stopped 60% (3/5); immediate endoscopy in unstable patients 100% (4/4).

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znac404.077.intervention: Education of doctors about the NICE quality standards for AUGIB management over a 1-year interval.

cycle2.result: Blatchford score used in 50% (11/22); endoscopy <24 hours in stable patients 53% (10/19); PPI for non-variceal bleeds 77% (17/22); aspirin stopped 80% (4/5); immediate endoscopy in unstable patients 100% (3/3).

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znac404.077.other_findings: Endoscopic management was fully compliant in both cycles (clips 100%; variceal bleeds all given terlipressin, antibiotics and band ligation). Time to endoscopy in stable patients worsened.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.37.topic: Aminoglycoside prescribing and level monitoring in neonates
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.37.setting: Two neonatal units in one Trust
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.37.standard: Trust Neonatal Infection Guideline: 100% adherence to criteria, amikacin 15 mg/kg, level at 24 hours before second dose, further doses only if level <5 mg/L or on pharmacist advice

cycle1.result: 100% adhered to guideline criteria and 100% prescribed 15 mg/kg; 12 (24%) had no level at 24 hours; of 38 with 24-hour levels only 6 (16%) were <5 mg/L; 17/23 (74%) in range at 36 hours; 2 patients received doses despite levels >5 mg/L.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.37.intervention: Recommended change from 24-hourly to 36-hourly dosing; re-audit planned in one year.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.37.other_findings: No direct correlation seen between gestational age, severity of illness and amikacin levels.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.21.standard: BSPGHAN guidelines: eleven azathioprine monitoring points (clinic attendance, height, weight, baseline VZV status, TPMT, and FBC, U&Es, amylase, CRP and LFT monitoring)

cycle1.result: Only 16 patients (19%) met all eleven points; 27 (24.5%) fully compliant with blood monitoring frequency; TPMT measured in 104 (97%) but late in 48 (46%); weight and height not documented in 31 (28%) and 47 (43%); baseline VZV not checked in 23 (21%).

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.21.intervention: Suggested shared-care guidelines, order sets with all parameters at diagnosis and a tick-box monitoring proforma for clinic.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.21.other_findings: Suboptimal monitoring correlated with living further from the centre (p=0.008) and tablet formulation (p=0.000); NHS England specialist commissioning rules prevent paediatric shared care.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.142.topic: Employment loss in early inflammatory arthritis

cycle1.result: 168 (10.1%) reported employment loss within three months; manual work IRR 1.82 (95% CI 1.37-2.42); direct effect after mediators IRR 1.54 (95% CI 1.15-2.06).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.142.other_findings: Disease activity, mental health and symptom burden together explained only 16.5% of the occupational effect.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11384.setting: MBT-I groups within Leicestershire Partnership NHS Trust

cycle1.dates: Cohorts in October 2023, July 2024 and February 2025
cycle1.result: Median attendance 8.5 sessions; inpatient admission during MBT-I 2.1%; 20.8% completed and referred for further therapy, 12.5% completed needing no further intervention; 22.9% did not complete and 37.5% did not commence.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11384.other_findings: Referrals mostly from secondary mental health services with minimal primary care referrals.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.41.standard: PHE Start Smart then Focus: blood culture before therapy, senior antimicrobial review at 48–72 hours, and IV to oral switch when set clinical criteria are met

cycle1.result: 100% had blood cultures within 72 hours of starting therapy; 82% had senior review at 48–72 hours; 46% eligible to switch to oral at 72 hours, of whom 33% were switched.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.41.intervention: Recommended an IV to oral switch guideline, education of pharmacists and nurses, and exploring hard stops on IV antimicrobials in the electronic system.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.41.other_findings: 55% had a positive blood culture. Small sample due to complex inclusion criteria and multiple hospital interfaces; need for better documentation of prescribing decisions.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.005.topic: Early inflammatory arthritis waiting times and DMARD start
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.005.setting: Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Foundation Trust rheumatology department, Preston
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.005.standard: NICE QS33: QS2 seen in rheumatology within 3 weeks of referral; QS3 newly diagnosed RA offered short-term glucocorticoids and combination DMARDs within 6 weeks of referral

cycle1.dates: First year of the NEIAA (dates not stated)
cycle1.result: 22 patients (8.9%) seen within 3 weeks of referral; 5 (7%) started DMARD within 6 weeks; mean wait 66 days (range 5-138) to be seen and diagnosed; 65 (90%) given bridging steroids; 65 (92%) started DMARDs.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.005.intervention: Process mapping and driver diagrams identified changes: primary care referral guidelines, more triage and new appointment capacity, simpler booking, text reminders, one-stop clinic with ultrasound, more drug education clinic capacity.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaa111.005.other_findings: 246 patients recruited, 71 with confirmed RA; 3-month follow-up forms completed in 61 (86%). Further waits of about 50 days if sent for investigations and 25–39 days for drug education.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10693.setting: Rohallion Clinic medium and low secure forensic psychiatry unit, Murray Royal Hospital, NHS Tayside
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10693.standard: Local and national guidance: 100% documented plan for oral and IM as-required medication; 100% offered oral before IM; 100% side-effect monitoring within 1 hour of rapid tranquillisation

cycle1.result: 38 (81%) had as-required medicines prescribed; 24 (63%) of these had a documented plan; reasons for IM medication and side-effect monitoring documented 25.42% of the time. Standards 1, 2 and 3 not met.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10693.intervention: Action plan: work with clinical team and pharmacist to improve documentation, and add headers to online assessment templates. Re-audit planned.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10693.other_findings: Lorazepam was most often prescribed, in line with local guidance; dosing frequency (mostly 4-hourly) was compliant.

cycle1.result: 33 internal referrals (18 from FLS, 7 COTE, 3 orthopaedics) and 71 GP referrals; commonest reason intolerance to oral medication (36), then declining BMD (14).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keae163.249.intervention: GPs advised to try alternative oral bisphosphonates or effervescent alendronic acid before referral; COTE team agreed to initiate and continue IV zoledronate.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keae163.249.other_findings: Workload review aimed to free rheumatology slots for early inflammatory arthritis.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.196.setting: 36 dermatology teams from 30 NHS trusts (national audit)
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.196.standard: BSDS sustainable skin surgery audit standards and checklist (scored out of 30), based on BSDS 2022 sustainability guidance

cycle1.result: Mean score 17.3/30 (95% CI 16.3–18.3; range 12–23); mean waste 1.0 kg per procedure; mean recycling rate 8.6%; 17/30 trusts (57%) had recycling bins; 19/30 (63%) had a mobile smoke evacuator.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.196.other_findings: Recycling rate was lower than the 16% in the 2022 study; Mohs lists generated more waste; trusts recycling single-use instruments had high recycling rates.

cycle1.result: Teriparatide (n=24): 17 (70%) had a documented post-teriparatide plan, 2 adverse events, no fractures after cessation. Romosozumab (n=26): 7 adverse events including heart failure and hypocalcaemia, no fractures after cessation. All met NICE criteria.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.094.other_findings: Most transitioned to zoledronic acid after anabolic therapy.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.135.topic: Early inflammatory arthritis waiting times and DMARD start
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.135.setting: Queen Elizabeth Hospital Birmingham rheumatology service, compared with national NEIAA data
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.135.standard: NICE RA quality standard 33: QS1 referral within 3 working days of primary care presentation; QS2 conventional DMARD within 6 weeks of referral

cycle1.dates: April 2018 to March 2024 (QEHB); May 2018 to March 2020 (national)
cycle1.result: QEHB QS1: 79% (115/146) White vs 21% (31/146) BAME referred within 3 days; QS2: 26.5% (27/102) BAME vs 73.5% (75/102) White. Nationally QS1 43% (12,561/29,417) White vs 47% (2,333/4,964) BAME; QS2 60% (723/1,204) BAME vs 57% (4,919/8,695) White.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.135.other_findings: 24% of QEHB patients were BAME vs 14% nationally; authors call for research into causes of ethnic disparities.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.068.setting: 36 dermatology teams from 30 NHS trusts (national audit)
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.068.standard: BSDS sustainable skin surgery audit standards and checklist (scored out of 30), based on BSDS 2022 sustainability guidance

cycle1.result: Mean score 17.3/30 (95% CI 16.3–18.3; range 12–23); mean waste 1.0 kg per procedure; mean recycling rate 8.6%; 17/30 trusts (57%) had recycling bins; 19/30 (63%) had a mobile smoke evacuator.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljae090.068.other_findings: Recycling rate was lower than the 16% in the 2022 study; Mohs lists generated more waste; trusts recycling single-use instruments had high recycling rates.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.47.topic: Influenza vaccination and asthma prescribing in children
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.47.setting: GP surgeries in Liverpool CCG (seven participating), primary care
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.47.standard: BTS/SIGN British guideline on the management of asthma 2016 for prescribing; influenza vaccine uptake

cycle1.result: 148 (31.2%) had flu vaccination; 194/297 (65.3%) prescriptions followed BTS guidelines.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314584.47.other_findings: Commonest non-compliance was salbutamol monotherapy or no medication. Low deprivation and age 5 or under associated with higher vaccination (p<0.05).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.015.topic: Self-management advice in early inflammatory arthritis
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.015.setting: Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Foundation Trust rheumatology department, Preston
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.015.standard: NICE QS33 QS4: RA patients offered educational and self-management activities within 1 month of diagnosis

cycle1.dates: Second year of the NEIAA (dates not stated)
cycle1.result: All RA patients received written information at baseline; only 39 (71%) documented as given self-management advice at 3-month follow-up; 41 (56%) started DMARD within 6 weeks of referral.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.015.intervention: Driver diagrams with patient group input identified changes: agreed definition of self-management, patient activation measure, different delivery formats and expert patients.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.015.other_findings: Patients felt self-management advice within the first 3 months was too soon, questioning the QS target. 3-month follow-up available for 56 (77%).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.009.setting: Complex Musculoskeletal Clinic, rheumatology department, secondary care
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.009.standard: 2017 EULAR recommendations for the management of fibromyalgia

cycle1.result: Before referral: pharmacological treatment 34/50 (68%), physiotherapy 5/50 (10%), psychological input 3/50 (6%); referred to multidisciplinary pain management programme 4/50 (8%).

cycle2.result: Before referral: pharmacological treatment 71/82 (87%, p=0.008), physiotherapy 28/82 (34%, p=0.002), psychological input 16/82 (20%, p=0.03); referred to pain management programme 64/82 (78%, p<0.0001); all had pain and function assessed; psychosocial context assessed in 64/82 (78%); information given to 53 (65%).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.009.other_findings: All medication recommendations were EULAR compliant. Giving patients information about their condition was identified as an area for improvement.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.289.topic: Monocyte count in giant cell arteritis diagnosis
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.289.setting: Royal National Hospital for Rheumatic Diseases GCA clinic, Bath

cycle1.result: 109/301 (36%) diagnosed with GCA; monocyte count predictive of GCA (AUC 0.83, 95% CI 0.77-0.90, p<0.0001); cut-off ≥0.9 gave specificity >95% and positive LR of 10.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.289.other_findings: 55/301 had started glucocorticoids before baseline bloods; monocyte sensitivity dropped 20% after at least one glucocorticoid dose.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.456.setting: General adult psychiatry services, NHS Grampian
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.456.standard: MHRA valproate guidance and Pregnancy Prevention Programme, including completed Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form

cycle1.result: 97% in contact with psychiatry services; only one patient (3%) had an ARAF completed and scanned to e-notes.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.456.intervention: Teams contacted by telephone and email and encouraged to complete the documentation.

cycle2.result: Completed ARAF in 21 patients; completion rose from 3% to 54%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2022.456.other_findings: 66% of women in cycle 1 were aged 45–60.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.25.standard: MHRA May 2014 drug safety update and NPPG May 2015 statement on domperidone (dose, duration, indication, ECG monitoring in high risk, non-pharmacological trial in GORD)

cycle1.dates: 1 January 2014 to before the NPPG alert (May 2015)
cycle1.result: Dose 43/50 (86%); duration 6/50 (12%); indication 9/50 (18%); ECG monitoring in high risk 12/33 (36%); non-pharmacological trial in GORD 11/17 (64%).

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.25.intervention: National MHRA and NPPG alerts on domperidone.

cycle2.result: Dose 10/10 (100%); duration 1/10 (10%); indication 1/10 (10%); ECG monitoring 0/4 (0%); non-pharmacological trial 2/3 (66%).

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2017-314585.25.other_findings: Cardiac monitoring in at-risk patients remained poor; many children still received domperidone off-licence long term.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/kead104.151.setting: Royal National Hospital for Rheumatic Diseases, Royal United Hospitals Bath
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/kead104.151.standard: NICE NG100 rheumatoid arthritis annual review standards

cycle1.dates: 12 months before an appointment in January 2019
cycle1.result: DAS28 documented 74.4% (253/340); erosions 42% (144/340); blood pressure 33% (113/340); mental health screen 7.9% (27/340); neck pain 14%; respiratory 21%; eye 21%; bone health 27.9% (95/340); AHP referral considered 38%; HAQ 22%.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/kead104.151.intervention: Planned digital RA annual review tool incorporating PROMs.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/kead104.151.other_findings: Variation between clinicians in documentation; VAS recorded in 73% (248/340).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.359.setting: Occupational therapy rheumatology service, Glasgow Royal Infirmary

cycle1.result: Mean BMI 33.5 kg/m²; 38% BMI >35; only around half of letters for BMI >30 recorded weight, and none discussed weight management plans or referrals.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.359.intervention: Recommended training for rheumatology staff on raising weight and better BMI recording.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.359.other_findings: Mean 5.2 comorbidities and 6.6 medications per patient; fatigue reported by 61%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11663.setting: Three adult mental health inpatient units (East, Central, West), Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11663.standard: NCISH, NHS CQUIN and Welsh Crisis Care Concordat: follow-up within 72 hours of discharge and discharge documentation of risk, MSE, medication and care plan

cycle1.result: Previous regional audit found variable compliance and incomplete documentation.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11663.intervention: Initial quality improvement measures (not detailed) after the first audit; standardised electronic templates, discharge checklists, automated alerts and audit feedback introduced.

cycle2.result: 72-hour follow-up 78.4% (29/37); discharge plan 86.5%; MSE 78.8%; risk assessment 72.7%; medication 63.6%. Modest improvement from baseline.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11663.other_findings: Central site 100% follow-up; East 57% with medication documentation 20%; West 66.7% with risk recorded in 46.2%.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.016.topic: Early inflammatory arthritis waiting times and DMARD start
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.016.setting: Lancashire and South Cumbria NHS Foundation Trust rheumatology department, Preston
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.016.standard: NICE QS33: QS2 seen within 3 weeks of referral; QS3 RA started on DMARDs within 6 weeks of referral

cycle1.result: 10% of all patients seen within 3 weeks; 7% of RA cohort (n=77) started DMARD within 6 weeks.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.016.intervention: Primary care referral guidelines, prompts for RF/CCP requests and changed antibody report wording, more triage and new appointment capacity (extra consultant, upskilled ESP), simpler booking, more drug education and monitoring clinic capacity, signposting to NRAS.

cycle2.result: 54% seen within 3 weeks; 56% of RA cohort (n=73) started DMARD within 6 weeks.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.016.other_findings: Remission/low disease activity at 3 months rose from 54% (year 1) to 69% (year 2); baseline disease activity was lower in year 2.

cycle1.result: 24 PJP cases; 79% on methotrexate, 70% on glucocorticoids; lymphopenia in 75%; 18/24 needed HDU/ICU and 7 died; only one on prophylaxis at diagnosis.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaf142.054.other_findings: Regular audits of BSR PJP prophylaxis in vasculitis on cyclophosphamide since 2016 may explain few cases in that group.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11825.setting: East Bromley Intensive Case Management in Psychosis team, Oxleas NHS Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11825.standard: 2024 MHRA valproate guidance including male patients: risk discussion, contraception advice, informed consent, MHRA materials, dual-signed ARAF

cycle1.result: Risk discussions 37% (F 80%, M 17%); contraception advice 15% (F 80%, M 3%); informed consent 61% (F 80%, M 20%); MHRA materials 11% (F 60%, M 6%); dual-signed ARAF in eligible females 0%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11825.intervention: Clinician education, 26 structured outpatient reviews, distribution of MHRA materials and a live ARAF tracking system.

cycle2.result: Male cohort: risk discussions 17%→87%; contraception advice 3%→83%; informed consent 20%→87%; MHRA materials 6%→83%; 100% of eligible females reviewed for second-consultant sign-off.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11825.other_findings: 13% of patients switched to alternative treatments after structured reviews and 9% were considering alternatives.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaf142.168.setting: Six institutions in five countries (Myositis Audit and Research Collaborative)
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaf142.168.country: Multinational (Australia, Brazil, Hong Kong and others)
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaf142.168.standard: IMACS guidelines for malignancy screening in idiopathic inflammatory myopathies

cycle1.result: Full IMACS screening panel received by 7.5% of high-risk, 6.6% of intermediate-risk and 27.5% of standard-risk patients; 9.1% of high-risk patients had annual screening for 3 years as recommended.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keaf142.168.other_findings: Over-screening seen in intermediate-risk (6.0%), standard-risk (6.6%) and IBM/JDM (41.2%) cohorts; following IMACS would raise screening costs 1.5-2.9-fold.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11562.setting: Inpatient psychiatric units, Hamad Hospital (Hamad Medical Corporation)
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11562.standard: Institutional Smoking Cessation Policy (smoking status, dependence severity, NRT initiation and monitoring, education, referral, discharge planning)

cycle1.result: Initial nicotine dependence screening >97%; dependence severity documented in 30.2%; appropriate NRT strength 12.3%; NRT side-effect monitoring 0%; 20% of smokers received NRT; Tobacco Control Center referral 18%; motivational interventions 1.8%; patient/family education 0%; NRT on discharge summary 3.3%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11562.intervention: Recommended targeted staff training, better access to educational resources and structured monitoring and documentation systems.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11562.other_findings: About 40% of admitted patients were current smokers; 29% declined NRT.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.007.setting: North Staffordshire Fracture Liaison Service, Midlands Partnership Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.007.standard: FLS policy (in line with national guidance) that patients aged 85 or over with fragility fracture are started empirically on oral bisphosphonate by the GP

cycle1.dates: Fractures December 2018 to October 2020; audited October 2020
cycle1.result: 160 (40%) had a bisphosphonate prescribed; over 90% alendronic acid.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.007.intervention: The standard GP recommendation letter was rewritten using GP feedback to address barriers, including advice on relative contraindications and referral.

cycle2.dates: Fractures December 2020 to May 2021; audited July 2021

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.007.other_findings: Median time from fracture to assessment was shorter in cycle 2 (5 vs 9 months), which may partly explain the rise.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.037.setting: Mater Dei Hospital (Clinical Genetics Laboratory records)

cycle1.result: Initial follow-up within 6 months 54.1% (33); 3-monthly SAA/CRP with dose escalation 8.3% (2/24); 6-monthly monitoring 31.2% (19); SAA and CK on yearly bloods 20.9% and 12.5%; no 3-monthly SAA/CRP during dose reduction.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.037.other_findings: Diagnostic delay over 10 years in 29.5%; colchicine delayed over 1 month after genetic diagnosis in 18.0%; no patients received canakinumab.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znac404.056.setting: Torbay and South Devon NHS Trust
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znac404.056.standard: Joint ESGAR/EAES/EFISDS/ESGE guidelines on gallbladder polyp management

cycle1.result: 86% appropriately offered surgery for polyps ≥10 mm; 40% with polyps >5 mm and risk factors not offered cholecystectomy; 44% without risk factors not offered appropriate follow-up; all without risk factors with polyps ≤5 mm appropriately managed.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znac404.056.intervention: Recommended unified local or national guidelines and multidisciplinary consensus.
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znac404.056.other_findings: Most patients with polyps ≤5 mm and risk factors were not offered ultrasound surveillance.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.15.topic: Outsourced clinical trial medicine delivery times
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.15.setting: Hospital clinical trials unit without onsite aseptic unit
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.15.standard: IMP arrival at the clinical trials unit by 1300h (later arrival defined as delayed treatment)

cycle1.dates: Six to twelve months (dates not stated)
cycle1.result: Manufacturing unit 1: 33 items, 71.86% late. Manufacturing unit 2: 23 items, 30% late (mostly due to late prescribing at site).

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.15.intervention: Recommended agreed KPIs with third-party suppliers, scoping local aseptic manufacture, and timely prescribing.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2023-nppg.15.other_findings: The closer unit (5.9 miles vs 63 miles) had fewer late deliveries.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11655.setting: Psychiatric intensive care unit, South West Yorkshire Partnership NHS Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11655.standard: SWYT seclusion and long-term segregation policy and seclusion toolkit (medical review within 1 hour, 4-hourly reviews, first MDT, independent MDT within 8-18 hours, daily reviews)

cycle1.result: First MDT within 08:00–22:00 next day 92.7%; out-of-hours reviews adherent 95%; daily non-RC medical reviews 87.2%; independent MDT reviews 24.2%; resident doctor review within 1 hour 64.4%; daily MDT reviews 66.6%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11655.intervention: Recommended prompts for independent MDT reviews, seclusion toolkit in new doctors' induction and discussion with RCs on documentation.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11655.other_findings: Low daily MDT review figure was linked to incorrect documentation on the seclusion proforma.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.175.setting: Community (primary care) ANA requests across West of Scotland, tested at Queen Elizabeth University Hospital

cycle1.result: 605 (19.67%) positive; 190 (31.57%) of positives referred; new CTD diagnosed in 38 patients; 314 (51.9%) of positives were 1/80 homogeneous.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.175.intervention: Recommended clearer testing guidelines and targeted education for primary care clinicians.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keag121.175.other_findings: Testing cost approximately £41,393 with low diagnostic yield.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11747.setting: Medway Community Mental Health Team (Gillingham, Chatham, Rochester localities)

cycle1.result: Report completion Chatham 66.7%, Gillingham 73.3%, Rochester 33%; capacity forms completed in over two-thirds (100% Rochester to 66% Chatham); completion 73% and 50% for the two responsible clinicians.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11747.intervention: Centralised communication system, improved documentation access and enhanced administrative processes; further audit planned.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11747.other_findings: Only three of six clinicians completed reports; reports clustered around review dates.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.19.topic: Analgesia in sickle cell pain crisis
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.19.setting: Paediatric inpatient admissions in one Trust
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.19.standard: 100% prescribed regular paracetamol and NSAIDs unless contraindicated (NICE CG143, BCSH); 100% prescribed appropriate doses by weight and age per local policy

cycle1.result: 45% (95% CI 31.9%–58.1%) prescribed regular analgesia; 78% (95% CI 67.9%–88.9%) prescribed appropriate doses. Neither standard met.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.19.intervention: Recommended education and training, an integrated care pathway booklet and a compulsory weight field on electronic prescribing.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.19.other_findings: Incorrect doses were due to wrong weights on the electronic system (n=4) and age-only dosing (n=8).

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljaf085.183.setting: Milton Keynes University Hospital, district general hospital
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljaf085.183.standard: BAD national non-melanoma skin cancer excision audit 2016 benchmarks (concordance 95%, complete excision ~98%); RCPath 10-day histology target; 28-day faster diagnosis standard

cycle1.result: Clinical–histological concordance 91%; complete excision with good margins 83% (involved margins 6%); only 22% of histology reports within 10 days (mean 33 days); mean 8 days from report to outcome communication; 9.5% considered for Mohs though 48% anatomically suitable.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljaf085.183.intervention: Recommended referral documentation templates, GP awareness of routine referral for low-risk BCC, a dermatology surgical logbook and better local access to Mohs surgery.
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljaf085.183.other_findings: 45% of referral types were undocumented; 36% came via the 2-week-wait pathway.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.021.setting: West Suffolk NHS Foundation Trust rheumatology, district general hospital

cycle1.result: Active synovitis in 17 (40%); 27 (63%) had DMARD started or switched after ultrasound; fibromyalgia patients less likely to escalate (8/20, 40% vs 19/23, 82.6%; p=0.004).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.021.other_findings: Synovitis on ultrasound was associated with DMARD escalation (82.4% vs 50%, p=0.03); ultrasound avoided escalation in a sizeable proportion.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.013.topic: Falls and bone health assessment after fracture
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.013.setting: University College London Hospital, central London
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.013.standard: 2017 NOGG guidelines, NICE CG161 falls in older people, and local hospital osteoporosis screening policy

cycle1.result: Only 5 (12%) had a full falls assessment. Osteoporosis assessment in 8/8 (100%) NOF vs 9/35 (25.7%) non-NOF; FRAX in 3/8 (37.5%) vs 3/35 (8.6%); referral to bone health clinic 1/8 vs 0/35.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.013.intervention: Planned education programme and a standardised proforma embedded in the electronic record.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keab247.013.other_findings: Lying/standing BP recorded in 37.5% NOF and 14.3% non-NOF; hip fracture patients had more complete assessments than other fractures.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10653.topic: Antipsychotic physical health monitoring in children
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10653.standard: NICE guidance on baseline investigations and monitoring for children and young people on antipsychotics; TEWV (2024) Psychotropic Monitoring Guide

cycle1.result: Overall compliance below 50%; side-effect assessment at 3 months 80%; ECG consideration/completion at 12 months 100%; weight, height, growth chart, waist, BP, HR, bloods and pre-treatment ECG below 80%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10653.intervention: Recommended improved handover between teams, better communication and documentation with GPs, and agreement on where to record monitoring data.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2025.10653.other_findings: No physical health clinic in the team; bloods and ECGs requested from GPs and results hard to track.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11731.setting: Meadowbrook Unit inpatient mental health unit, Salford, Greater Manchester Mental Health NHS Foundation Trust
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11731.standard: Trust seclusion policy: eight core medical review criteria plus two best-practice criteria

cycle1.result: No reviews met all eight criteria; most common number met was one (n=9). Physical health 70%, psychiatric health 40%, medication side effects 0%, harms of seclusion 2%, decision to continue 97%, steps to end seclusion 25%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11731.intervention: Local teaching and presentations, communication to line managers and posters of trust standards in clinical areas.

cycle2.result: Seven reviews met all eight criteria; most common number met was four or five (n=12). Physical health 82%, psychiatric health 66%, medication side effects 19%, harms of seclusion 14%, decision to continue 91%, steps to end seclusion 23%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11731.other_findings: Small declines in documenting the decision to continue and steps to end seclusion; asleep, senior-led and undocumented reviews may have affected 2025 results.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.093.topic: Employment loss in early inflammatory arthritis
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.093.setting: National Early Inflammatory Arthritis Audit, rheumatology services in England and Wales

cycle1.result: 5999 (48%) in paid work; at diagnosis 171 (4.7%) had stopped work and 336 (9.2%) changed jobs due to EIA; absenteeism in 685 (29.5%). Good EULAR response at 3 months associated with improved work outcomes (p<0.001).

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.093.other_findings: Semi-routine and routine workers were more likely to stop work.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11677.topic: Sodium monitoring on antidepressants in older adults
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11677.setting: Psychiatry of Old Age inpatient unit, North Dublin Mental Health Services for Older Persons
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11677.standard: NICE and Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines: serum sodium monitoring 2–4 weeks after antidepressant initiation or dose change in high-risk patients

cycle1.result: Baseline U&E on admission in all patients; follow-up within 2–4 weeks of initiation in 50%; U&E within four weeks of dose escalation in 16%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11677.intervention: Reminder stickers placed in each patient's file and educational discussion with the MDT. Second cycle underway.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11677.other_findings: Mirtazapine and venlafaxine were the most common antidepressants; 50% had dose increases during admission.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.071.topic: COVID-19 vaccination in patients on biologics

cycle1.result: 329 received two doses, 8 one dose and 15 (4.3%) unvaccinated; 146 had mild side effects; 3 (2.1%) grade 3 or above; 15 (10%) reported arthritis flare.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keac133.071.other_findings: Reasons for declining included fear of reactions or flares and mistrust of the vaccine.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keae163.050.setting: Royal Berkshire Hospital rheumatology, district general hospital

cycle1.result: Side-effect discussion documented at baseline in <10%; 2% MACE and 3% herpes zoster; 36% discontinued; remission or significant reduction in disease activity in 64%.

DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keae163.050.intervention: Recommended better patient education before starting treatment.
DOI:10.1093/rheumatology/keae163.050.other_findings: 43% had failed two or three biologics before a JAK inhibitor; 64% started on baricitinib.

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljad113.002.standard: BAD 2016 UK guidelines for management of SJS/TEN in adults, audit standards

cycle1.result: Within 24 h: SCORTEN 52% (76/147), medication list 77% (113), medication timelines 71% (104). Initial assessment: eyes by ophthalmologist 48% (71), mouth 88% (130), genital skin 70% (103), urinary tract 63% (93). Daily assessments in first 10 days: mouth 18%, eyes 8%, urinary tract and genital skin 10%. Culprit drug avoidance advice 58% (76/130); medic alert request 6% (9/147).

DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljad113.002.intervention: Suggested an assessment and clinical review checklist.
DOI:10.1093/bjd/ljad113.002.other_findings: Drug causality assessment was documented adequately; 29% of UK dermatology centres took part.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.21.topic: Measurable oral liquid doses in children
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.21.setting: Paediatric inpatient areas in one Trust (paper and electronic prescribing)
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.21.standard: Local dispensing standard: prescribed volumes measurable on the printed graduations of one oral syringe

cycle1.result: Electronic prescriptions: 61/257 (24%) not measurable; paper charts: 57/303 (19%) not measurable (p=0.19). 77 of 457 liquid doses needed up to 4% adjustment and 10 up to 9%; 19/560 (3.4%) needed measuring to two decimal places.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.21.intervention: Recommended dose rounding at prescribing and adding liquid strength information to local guidelines.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2016-311535.21.other_findings: Frequently non-measurable drugs included diazepam, alimemazine, chloral hydrate, azithromycin, metronidazole, paracetamol and ibuprofen; the electronic system had no automatic rounding.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11570.setting: Inpatient addiction ward, Allied Hospital II, Faisalabad
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11570.standard: Predefined standards from NICE guidance, Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines and international recommendations

cycle1.result: Met targets: stimulant history 94.7%, temporal relationship 89.5%, exclusion of delirium 100%, baseline observations 94.7%, MSE 94.7%, prescribing details 100%. Below target: toxicology 42.1%, blood glucose 52.6%, structured risk assessment 78.9%, de-escalation 73.7%, medication safety checks 78.9%, post-medication monitoring 84.2%, reassessment 73.7%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11570.intervention: Standardised MIP admission checklist and targeted staff education; re-audit planned.
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11570.other_findings: MIP accounted for 19/82 (23.2%) of inpatient addiction admissions, ranging 18.2% to 33.3% per month.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf159.015.topic: Surgical site infection surveillance in hip fracture
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf159.015.setting: Irish Hip Fracture Database, national clinical audit across Irish hospitals

cycle1.dates: First full year of data received May 2024
cycle1.result: Overall SSI incidence <1%; SSI increased length of stay from 19 to 34 days; completeness of additional variables 68 to 100%.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf159.015.intervention: SSI dataset (ECDC-based) embedded into the IHFD portal after a three-hospital pilot, with monthly training webinars and infographics; dataset refined by PDSA.
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znaf159.015.other_findings: Hip fracture governance committees now include infection prevention and control members; quarterly SSI reports are sent to hospitals.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2019-nppc.39.standard: Aciclovir dosing per BNF for Children and trust empirical antibiotic guidelines

cycle1.result: 26% (9/35) of aciclovir doses incorrect; wrong drop-down option chosen in 78% (7/9) of incorrect prescriptions.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2019-nppc.39.intervention: Aciclovir drop-down options in the electronic prescribing system reordered so the most frequently used option appeared first (from 01/02/17).

cycle2.result: 17% (5/30) of doses incorrect; wrong drop-down option in 0% (0/5) of incorrect prescriptions.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2019-nppc.39.other_findings: Error rate was 14% (7/50) when the correct drop-down was chosen vs 47% (7/15) when the wrong option was selected.

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.14.topic: Proton pump inhibitor prescribing in children
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.14.standard: Trust guidance: lansoprazole capsules/orodispersible tablets first line; three standards (appropriate PPI, documented indication, appropriate dose)

cycle1.result: Appropriate PPI 76%; documented indication 88%; appropriate dose 100%. Infants and toddlers had the lowest appropriate PPI choice (63%).

DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.14.intervention: Recommended clinicians monitor prescribing and switch omeprazole suspension to lansoprazole where appropriate.
DOI:10.1136/archdischild-2020-nppg.14.other_findings: Lansoprazole accounted for 64 (77%) prescriptions; 12% had no documented indication.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11571.setting: Inpatient psychiatry ward, Allied Hospital II, Faisalabad
DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11571.standard: Pre-RT standards from NICE guidance, Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines and BAP/NAPICU consensus

cycle1.result: De-escalation documented 71%; clear indication 83%; pre-RT workup 47%; baseline observations 85%; capacity/consent 90%; cardiac/QT risk 85% (haloperidol); reassessment before repeat dosing 42%; airway risk 78% (benzodiazepines); contraindications/interactions 66%.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11571.intervention: Structured pre-RT checklist and staff education.

cycle2.result: De-escalation 92%; clear indication 96%; pre-RT workup 85%; reassessment before repeat dosing 92%; airway risk 92%; contraindications 85%; other domains met or exceeded standards.

DOI:10.1192/bjo.2026.11571.other_findings: Medication details were documented in 100% at baseline.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.133.setting: Two district general hospitals, Frimley Health NHS Foundation Trust; day case laparoscopic cholecystectomy and inguinal hernia repair
DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.133.standard: GIRFT guidelines for day case discharge prescribing (analgesia, antiemetics, laxatives)

cycle1.result: 25% of patients received the correct discharge medications.

DOI:10.1093/bjs/znae197.133.intervention: Pre-populated discharge medication order set created in the EPIC electronic record.

cycle2.result: 83% of patients received the correct discharge medications.
